quote: Ladies and gentlemen of the class of '97: Wear sunscreen.

earliest.author: Mary Schmich
earliest.work: Column "Advice, like youth, probably just wasted on the young", Chicago Tribune
earliest.wording: Ladies and gentlemen of the class of '97: Wear sunscreen.

notes: Schmich's column was written as a graduation speech. By early August 1997 an e-mail was passing it around as Vonnegut's commencement address at MIT, where he never gave one. Schmich set the record straight in a column on August 3, 1997.

quote: A lie can travel halfway around the world while the truth is putting on its shoes.

earliest.work: The Portland Gazette (Portland, Maine), an untitled article
earliest.wording: for falsehood will fly from Maine to Georgia, while truth is pulling her boots on.

notes: The saying was in print, in quotation marks and with no name, fifteen years before Twain was born. It grew from an older idea: Jonathan Swift wrote in 1710 that "Falsehood flies, and the Truth comes limping after it". A 1919 magazine credited a version to Twain, who had died in 1910, and Churchill was credited by 1981. Quote Investigator found no support for either.

quote: Be kind, for everyone you meet is fighting a hard battle.

earliest.author: Ian Maclaren (John Watson)
earliest.work: The Congregationalist (Boston), quoting a Christmas message Maclaren sent to The British Weekly
earliest.wording: Be pitiful, for every man is fighting a hard battle.

notes: Ian Maclaren was the pen name of the minister John Watson. His message was probably printed in England just before Christmas 1897. The wording with "kind" was in print by 1957, still credited to Maclaren. Fred Shapiro called the credit to Plato anachronistic by almost 2,500 years.

quote: It is not the strongest of the species that survives, nor the most intelligent, but the one most responsive to change.

earliest.author: Leon C. Megginson
earliest.work: Presidential address "Lessons from Europe for American Business", printed in Southwestern Social Science Quarterly 44:1 (June 1963)
earliest.wording: it is not the most intellectual of the species that survives; it is not the strongest that survives; but the species that survives is the one that is able best to adapt and adjust to the changing environment in which it finds itself

notes: Megginson, a management professor, gave his own reading of Darwin without quotation marks. In January 1964 he wrote "so says Charles Darwin", and later versions were shortened and presented as Darwin's own words. The Darwin Correspondence Project calls it a misquotation.

quote: First they ignore you, then they laugh at you, then they fight you, then you win.

earliest.author: Nicholas Klein
earliest.work: Speech to the Third Biennial Convention of the Amalgamated Clothing Workers of America, Baltimore
earliest.wording: First they ignore you. Then they ridicule you. And then they attack you and want to burn you. And then they build monuments to you.

notes: Klein was a union representative. Sayings about the stages a new idea goes through were older, from the nineteenth century. A 1982 article in the magazine WIN credited a version to Gandhi, who died in 1948. Quote Investigator found no support for that credit.

quote: Premature optimization is the root of all evil.

earliest.author: Donald Knuth
earliest.work: Structured Programming with go to Statements, Computing Surveys 6:4
earliest.wording: We should forget about small efficiencies, say about 97% of the time: premature optimization is the root of all evil.

notes: Knuth wrote it in a paper on go to statements, in a passage about where programmers should spend effort on speed. The journal issue is dated December 1974.

quote: Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic.

earliest.author: Arthur C. Clarke
earliest.work: Letter to Science, "Clarke's Third Law on UFO's" (vol. 159, no. 3812)
earliest.wording: Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic.

notes: Clarke's third law. He added it in a footnote to the 1973 revision of his essay "Hazards of Prophecy" in Profiles of the Future.

earliest.author: René Descartes
earliest.work: Discours de la méthode, part four
earliest.wording: cette vérité, je pense, donc je suis, étoit si ferme et si assurée

notes: I think, therefore I am. Descartes published the Discourse in French in 1637. The Latin form, cogito, ergo sum, is better known but came later.

quote: Wenn ich wüsste, dass morgen die Welt untergeht, würde ich heute noch ein Apfelbäumchen pflanzen.

earliest.work: Circular letter by the Hessian pastor Karl Lotz to the Confessing Church in Kurhessen-Waldeck
earliest.wording: Und wenn morgen die Welt unterginge, so wollen wir heute unser Apfelbäumchen pflanzen.

notes: If I knew the world would end tomorrow, I would still plant an apple tree today. Lotz introduced it as a saying of Luther's, so it was already credited to him, nearly four centuries after Luther's death. The Lutherhaus Eisenach museum says Luther never wrote it. It spread from May 1950, after a radio feature by Thilo Koch.

quote: Be yourself; everyone else is already taken.

earliest.work: Anonymous Usenet message in a newsgroup used mostly by people in the Netherlands
earliest.wording: Be yourself. Everyone else is already taken.

notes: Wilde wrote several quips about identity and pretense, but none matches. Thomas Merton wrote a related thought in 1967. Soon after the 1999 post the saying was credited to a Gilbert Perreira, without evidence that he wrote it. Quote Investigator found no support for the credit to Wilde.
